content.text: ACID promises four things about the transactions you actually run: all or nothing, declared rules hold at commit, concurrent work is kept apart to the level you chose, and committed work survives a crash. It doesn't know your business rules, where a transaction should start and end, or what to do after an error. In a test on SQL Server 2022, a transfer wrapped in
failed halfway and still committed the debit.
A support ticket says Mona sent 100 to Karim, got an error, and her balance dropped anyway. Karim got nothing. The transfer runs between
on a fully ACID database. In a test on SQL Server 2022, Karim's wallet held 950 and a

constraint caps every wallet at 1,000, so the credit failed with error 547. The application received that error as an exception. Yet the debit was committed: Mona had 400, Karim still had 950, and 100 had left the system.
The belief: if the database is ACID, the data stays correct, whatever the application does with transactions.

It's an understandable shortcut. The acronym reads like a warranty, and one of its letters literally stands for consistency. Most writes are single statements, and a single statement really is all or nothing, so the guarantee seems to hold everywhere. Frameworks add to the feeling: EF Core wraps one
call in a transaction for you, so many developers never decide where a transaction begins or ends.
is four promises, and each one has a boundary. Everything outside those boundaries is still your job.
Atomicity covers the transaction you opened, not the one you meant
Atomicity means all of a transaction's changes are applied, or none are. The database can only apply that to the transaction it sees. Without an explicit transaction, SQL Server runs in
: each statement is its own transaction, committed as soon as it completes. PostgreSQL does the same, wrapping each statement in an implicit
. Two updates sent one after the other are two transactions, and a failure between them leaves the first one committed.
An error doesn't always end the transaction
This is what bit the transfer. In SQL Server,

by default, and Microsoft's docs say that in some cases only the statement that raised the error is rolled back and the transaction continues. In the test, the failed credit was undone, the next statement was

, and it committed the debit. PostgreSQL handles errors differently: its docs say an error puts the transaction block in an aborted state. That behavior is quoted from the docs; only SQL Server ran for this article.
Consistency means your declared rules, not your intentions
Microsoft's definition says a completed transaction must leave data in a consistent state, with "all rules" applied to its changes. Those rules are the ones you declared: keys, foreign keys,

. The database has no idea that a transfer must not change the total amount of money, or that an order can't ship before it's paid. The same guide is blunt about it: applications are responsible for starting and ending transactions at points that enforce the logical consistency of the data. In the test, the
constraint did its job perfectly. The transaction boundary and error handling were the bug.
Isolation is a level you choose
Microsoft's definition of isolation describes serializability: concurrent transactions end up as if they had run one after another. The default you get is weaker. SQL Server's default is

, which Microsoft's own table lists as allowing nonrepeatable reads and phantoms. Two requests that read a balance and write it back can also overwrite each other, a lost update this path covers in its own article. A later article explains what each

Durable means a committed transaction survives a crash: PostgreSQL's tutorial says the changes are logged to permanent storage before the commit is reported. It also means a wrong commit is just as permanent as a right one. And durability can be relaxed: SQL Server 2014 and later support delayed durable transactions, which commit before the log record reaches disk.
